Previous research has recommended a sampling frequency of at least 1000hz for CMJ force-time 
measurements (14, 20, 26, 27). Additionally, exporting and analyzing the unfiltered or raw 
vertical force data has been recommended over the filtered force time data due to the possibility 
of underestimation of CMJ height (26, 27). The athlete was instructed to stand with one foot on 
each platform with their hands on their hips. To prevent injury, the platforms were surrounded 
by a foam platform of the same height as the force platform. The athlete was asked to stand still 
for a period of 3 seconds to allow the system to ascertain body weight and the onset of movement 
threshold (14, 20). Once the system had recorded body weight, the athlete was instructed to 
jump as high as they could while keeping their hands on their hips. For each jump the athlete 
was required to return to the “quiet standing” position with the hands remaining on the hips 
for 3 seconds in order for the system to again ascertain body weight and the onset of movement 
threshold before performing a second trial. If the athlete failed to keep their hands on the hips 
during the jump, or the athlete did not land on the force platform, the jump did not count and 
was not considered successful. Two attempts were given for each athlete. If for any reason a 
jump was unsuccessful, the athlete was required to perform additional jumps until they had 
achieved two successful jumps that were recorded and saved by the system. 
 
Athlete height (cm) was recorded by a member of the athletic performance staff. Force- Decks 
software (Vald Performance, Newstead, QLD, AUS) was utilized to collect and 
process/extrapolate the force-time data into commonly used discrete variables. Discrete values 
from the trial attempt in which the athlete jumped the highest (using flight time method) were 
utilized for analysis. Concentric-RPD100ms was measured as the change in power over the first 
100ms of the concentric phase. The flight time method of jump height calculation was calculated 
as jump height (cm) = (g*t2)/8. Where g is the acceleration due to gravity and t is the flight time. 
 
Statistical Analysis 
Univariate outliers were identified by transforming the univariate scores into z-scores. 
Multivariate outliers were identified and removed by finding Mahalanobis distances. Ten 
participants were identified as univariate and/or multivariate outliers and were not used for 
primary analyses. Primary analyses were conducted on the CMJ data from the remaining 265 
participants. A 2 x 2 multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) was used to determine 
whether significant differences in the three dependent variables of VJ height (cm), concentric 
RPD-100ms, and peak power existed between athletes at different playing levels. A discriminant 
function analysis (DFA) was used to investigate how the three dependent variables (jump 
height, peak power, and concentric rate of power development [concentric-RPD100ms]) or 
outcome variables may discriminate the participants based on a combined variables (sex and 
competition level). A description of the primary statistical tests conducted and the follow-up 
analyses are presented in Table 2. All statistics were conducted with IBM SPSS v.25. Alpha was 
set at p < .05 for all tests (IBM, New York, NY, USA)."

DISCUSSION 
 
The discriminant function analysis revealed one significant function (discriminant function 
#1/DF1; Table 4) which indicated that jump height and peak power discriminate between 
female athletes at NCAA DI institutions and NAIA institutions. These two variables can be 
viewed as an athlete’s ability to propel or accelerate their body vertically off the ground and 
produce power in multiple directions (i.e. jumping, sprinting, and change of direction ability). 
The DFA follow-up ANOVA showed a significant difference between all males and females 
regardless of competition level based on the scores from the DF1. The scores of females were 
also significantly different between the two competition levels. However, male scores were not 
significantly different based on the DF1 scores. Overall DF1 had a large effect on discriminating 
between the four groups (canonical R2 = .69. This metric is used to convey the effect size). The 
results displayed in the group centroid plots (Figure 1) and the DFA follow-up ANOVA 
indicates that the significant function could be indicative of strength differences between the 
participants. The findings of this study are believed to be the first to attempt to examine 
differences in athletes from NCAA DI and NAIA institutions based on performance variables 
recorded in the CMJ. 
 
The findings of this study based on the results of the MANOVA and follow-up univariate 
ANOVAs are that females at the DI level performed significantly better in the CMJ based on 
jump height, peak power and concentric RPD-100ms compared to females at the NAIA. The 
results displayed in Table 3 show that DI females jumped roughly 5cm higher with higher power"

38	    "text": "Int J Exerc Sci 13(6): 470-479, 2020 
International Journal of Exercise Science http://www.intjexersci.com 
477 
outputs and did so faster (RPD-100ms) than their NAIA counterparts. Previous research using 
female participants at different levels of NCAA competition has shown that DI athletes across 
different sports (soccer, volleyball, softball) had greater vertical jump heights than their DII or 
DIII counterparts (3, 22). The findings in this study showed that female DI athletes differed 
significantly from their NAIA counterparts in all performance variables measured. The previous 
literature on female participants at different collegiate competition levels did not report on peak 
power or concentric RPD-100ms. However, because jump height and power are correlated 
variables it would be likely that similar results would be seen in those populations. 
 
The findings of this study showed DI male participants obtained a higher vertical jump than 
NAIA males, however the difference was roughly 1cm (Table 3). This study is believed to be the 
first study to report peak power and concentric RPD-100ms for male athletes at the NCAA DI 
and NAIA levels. Only peak power was found to be significantly different between the two 
groups of males. However, it was noted that the NCAA DI group differed significantly in body 
mass for the NAIA group (Table 1). This body mass difference is most likely the reason for the 
observed difference in peak power, and although there was a difference in body mass, both 
groups obtained nearly the same jump height. This suggests that the two groups may not be as 
different in respect to physical performance as previously thought. Previous research has shown 
that male athletes from DI have jumped higher than their counterparts at DII or DIII (9, 10). 
Brummitt & Engillis (4) found that DIII and NAIA did not differ significantly in the single leg 
hop or standing long jump. Only one study was identified which reported vertical jump 
performance comparisons between NCAA DI and NAIA male athletes (23). The DI baseball 
players obtained higher vertical jump heights than their NAIA counterparts. The results of the 
current study show that females differed from males in all variables measured regardless of 
competition level. Given that females and males differ in body mass, this variable was not 
included as a covariate. Future research comparing athletes from different competition levels 
should include body mass in the analysis. In the current study, sport was not used as a covariate 
because the group sizes (n) based on sport were small. Further research should seek to obtain a 
sufficient number of participants to include sport as a covariate. One major limitation of the 
analysis is that Box’s M was violated (p < .001) which decreases the MANOVA’s trustworthiness. 
It is important to note that Field (8) warns of the disadvantage of using Box’s M particularly that 
it is very sensitive. Furthermore, the results of the univariate and multivariate analyses, in 
addition to the large squared canonical correlation show findings that are generally consistent. 
Thus, the researchers are confident that the outcomes of this study are trustworthy. 
 
The key message in this study is that significant differences in lower-body power measures from 
the CMJ were observed between males and females within their respective competition levels 
as well as between the two levels. Previously it has been suggested that NCAA DI athletes are 
the best athletes in collegiate athletics because DI is the top level of competition. Female DI 
athletes have previously outperformed their NCAA peers in measures of physical performance 
(3). The results found for female athletes in the present study further add to the previous 
research findings and may suggest that DI female athletes should be considered the best 
collegiate athletes. However, for male athletes more research should be conducted to confidently

    "text": "Original Research 
 
A Comparison of Lower Body Power Characteristics Between Collegiate 
Athletes from Different Competition Levels. 
 
CODY A. STAHL†1, KESTON G. LINDSAY‡2, J. BRYAN MANN‡3, MARGARET HUNT‡2, and J. 
JAY DAWES‡1 
 
1School of Kinesiology, Applied Health and Recreation, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, 
Oklahoma, USA; 2Helen and Arthur E. Johnson Beth-El College of Nursing and Health 
Sciences, University of Colorado Colorado Springs, Colorado Springs, Colorado, USA; 3School 
of Education and Human Development, University of Miami, Miami, Florida, USA. 
 
†Denotes graduate student author, ‡Denotes professional author 
ABSTRACT 
International Journal of Exercise Science 13(6): 470-479, 2020. The counter-movement jump (CMJ) is 
frequently utilized by strength and conditioning professionals working with athletes, given its relationship to a 
multitude of performance variables associated with success in sports. PURPOSE: To examine characteristics of CMJ 
performance between NAIA and NCAA Division I male and female athletes. METHODS: Archival data for 275 
student athletes from two NCAA Division 1 universities (NCAA DI; males = 84, females = 74) and one NAIA 
university (NAIA; males = 66, females = 51) were utilized for this analysis. The CMJ was performed utilizing a dual 
single axis (Pasco PS 2141 plates, sampling rate 1000hz unfiltered) force platform system. A 2 x 2 multivariate 
analysis of variance (MANOVA) was used to determine whether significant differences in the three dependent 
variables of VJ height (cm), concentric RPD-100ms, and peak power existed between athletes at different playing 
levels. RESULTS: A MANOVA revealed significant differences based on sex and competition level in the dependent 
variables measured (Wilk’s Lambda = 0.908, F(3,259) = 8.732, p < .001, partial η2 = .092). DISCUSSION: The findings 
of this study revealed that females at the Division I level achieved significantly greater jump heights, peak power 
and concentric RPD-100ms compared to females at the NAIA level. Division I males displayed significantly higher 
peak power than their NAIA counterparts. 
 
KEY WORDS: Counter-movement jump (CMJ), NCAA, NAIA 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
The National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) and the National Association of 
Intercollegiate Athletics (NAIA) are the two major governing bodies for collegiate athletics in 
the United States. Approximately 550,000 collegiate-athletes compete in the NCAA and NAIA 
(16, 17). Unlike the NAIA, which is mainly comprised of one level of competition, the NCAA is 
made up of three distinctive divisions: Division I (DI), Division II (DII), and Division III (DIII). 
Anecdotally, one would anticipate that NCAA DI athletes are superior to their DII & DIII as well 
as their NAIA counterparts due to those institutions having the ability to provide more benefits"
  },
  {
    "page": 2,
    "text": "Int J Exerc Sci 13(6): 470-479, 2020 
International Journal of Exercise Science http://www.intjexersci.com 
471 
to athletes, thanks in part to national notoriety and larger athletic budgets (i.e., more money for 
facilities and scholarships; 16, 17). However, this supposition is largely speculative as relatively 
few studies have compared performance on predictors of athletic success between athletes in 
these organizations (3, 4, 9, 23). 
 
Levels of lower-body power have been shown to effectively discriminate between different 
levels of competition in a range of sports including American Football, rugby league, volleyball, 
and ice hockey (1). In a study by Fry and Kraemer (9) it was discovered that vertical jump 
performance was significantly greater among Division I football players compared to Division 
II and III players. Similarly, Barnes et al. (3) found that Division I female volleyball players had 
significantly greater countermovement jump heights than their peers at the Division II and III 
levels. However, little data has been published comparing performance on field based tests 
between NCAA and NAIA athletes. 
 
Brummit and Engillis (4) reported NAIA male basketball players jumped further in the single 
leg hop (left leg; p < .05) than NCAA DIII male basketball players. Spaniol (23) reported that DI 
baseball players obtained higher vertical jump heights than NAIA players. However, it is 
important to note that in his review, Spaniol (23) used normative data from previously 
published abstracts to make these comparisons (24, 25). Neither the comparison review (23) nor 
the previously published abstracts stated what type of vertical jump test (i.e. countermovement 
jump, squat jump, jump and reach) was used for measurement. Based on the limited amount of 
data available, further research is required to better understand the physical performance 
differences between collegiate athletes competing at different levels. By developing a profile for 
athletes at different levels of play, coaches may be able to assess an athlete’s potential for success 
at a specific level of play, which may assist in team recruitment and retention decisions. 
 
The countermovement jump (CMJ) is a practical and reliable performance test frequently used 
to measure an athlete’s lower-body power (5, 13, 15). In fact, it is one of the most commonly 
used performance tests by coaches and researchers to indirectly measure power of the lower-
body (6). CMJ performance is typically assessed and reported as either jump height (an estimate 
of the height change in the athlete’s center of mass) or estimated peak power output (which can 
be calculated by inputting jump height into a validated equation such as the Sayers’ equation; 
12, 15, 21). The CMJ has previously been measured using a number of different devices such as 
contact mats, force platforms, infrared platforms, accelerometers or linear position transducers 
and even video analysis, though force platforms are often regarded as the ‘gold-standard’ for 
test accuracy (6, 11, 19). 
 
A common method for calculating jump height is to use flight time, which is the total duration 
the athlete spends in the air with no ground contact. The flight time method of calculation is 
typically utilized when measuring CMJ on contacts mats or force plates. Flight time does not 
start until the athlete loses contact with the jumping surface and stops the moment their foot 
contacts the landing surface (2, 6). Force platforms are able to directly measure ground reaction 
forces (GRFs) which are used to extrapolate or calculate additional variables such as velocity at 
different points during the movement, thereby providing a more robust measure of lower-body"
  },
  {
    "page": 3,
    "text": "Int J Exerc Sci 13(6): 470-479, 2020 
International Journal of Exercise Science http://www.intjexersci.com 
472 
power compared to other devices (19). The velocity and GRF values, in addition to jump height, 
can provide possible insight into an athlete’s physiological capabilities (force producing 
capabilities, neuromuscular coordination, and/or stretch shortening cycle (SSC) capabilities) 
which other instruments cannot provide. In order to fully understand and utilize the 
information obtained from lower body power measures, one should not only know how high 
an athlete can jump but also how they summate or produce force and how quickly that is 
accomplished (12). 
 
To the best of the investigator’s knowledge, a comparison of CMJ characteristics jump height, 
peak power, and concentric rate of power development-100ms (RPD-100ms) between athletes 
from the NCAA and NAIA has only been reported once (23). Furthermore, few research studies 
have provided concurrent normative data from NCAA Divisions and NAIA athletes in the same 
study. Therefore, the purpose of the present study is to (a) describe the relationship between 
CMJ characteristics and level of competition and (b) report descriptive data on jump 
performance for male and female athletes at the NAIA and NCAA DI levels. 
 
METHODS 
 
Participants 
Archival CMJ data for 275 student athletes from two NCAA division 1 universities (NCAA DI; 
males = 84, females = 74) and one NAIA university (NAIA; males = 66, females = 51) were 
utilized for this analysis. Descriptive variables such as age, height, and weight are presented in 
table 1. A post hoc power analysis conducted with G*POWER 3.1 (7) showed that with an alpha 
set at p < .05 the achieved power and effect size in the present study were 0.983 and 0.0494 
respectively. These data were collected by the athletic performance training staff for each 
university as part of routine athletic testing. All of the athletes in this sample reported being 
injury free within the 6 months prior to testing and completed an informed consent. Permission 
to conduct this study was provided by the Institutional Review Board from the University of 
Colorado Colorado Springs and University of Missouri. Based on the archival nature for this 
data, this study qualified for expedited review. This research was carried out fully in accordance 
to the ethical standards of the International Journal of Exercise Science (18).

Previous research has recommended a sampling frequency of at least 1000hz for CMJ force-time 
measurements (14, 20, 26, 27). Additionally, exporting and analyzing the unfiltered or raw 
vertical force data has been recommended over the filtered force time data due to the possibility 
of underestimation of CMJ height (26, 27). The athlete was instructed to stand with one foot on 
each platform with their hands on their hips. To prevent injury, the platforms were surrounded 
by a foam platform of the same height as the force platform. The athlete was asked to stand still 
for a period of 3 seconds to allow the system to ascertain body weight and the onset of movement 
threshold (14, 20). Once the system had recorded body weight, the athlete was instructed to 
jump as high as they could while keeping their hands on their hips. For each jump the athlete 
was required to return to the “quiet standing” position with the hands remaining on the hips 
for 3 seconds in order for the system to again ascertain body weight and the onset of movement 
threshold before performing a second trial. If the athlete failed to keep their hands on the hips 
during the jump, or the athlete did not land on the force platform, the jump did not count and 
was not considered successful. Two attempts were given for each athlete. If for any reason a 
jump was unsuccessful, the athlete was required to perform additional jumps until they had 
achieved two successful jumps that were recorded and saved by the system. 
 
Athlete height (cm) was recorded by a member of the athletic performance staff. Force- Decks 
software (Vald Performance, Newstead, QLD, AUS) was utilized to collect and 
process/extrapolate the force-time data into commonly used discrete variables. Discrete values 
from the trial attempt in which the athlete jumped the highest (using flight time method) were 
utilized for analysis. Concentric-RPD100ms was measured as the change in power over the first 
100ms of the concentric phase. The flight time method of jump height calculation was calculated 
as jump height (cm) = (g*t2)/8. Where g is the acceleration due to gravity and t is the flight time. 
 
Statistical Analysis 
Univariate outliers were identified by transforming the univariate scores into z-scores. 
Multivariate outliers were identified and removed by finding Mahalanobis distances. Ten 
participants were identified as univariate and/or multivariate outliers and were not used for 
primary analyses. Primary analyses were conducted on the CMJ data from the remaining 265 
participants. A 2 x 2 multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) was used to determine 
whether significant differences in the three dependent variables of VJ height (cm), concentric 
RPD-100ms, and peak power existed between athletes at different playing levels. A discriminant 
function analysis (DFA) was used to investigate how the three dependent variables (jump 
height, peak power, and concentric rate of power development [concentric-RPD100ms]) or 
outcome variables may discriminate the participants based on a combined variables (sex and 
competition level). A description of the primary statistical tests conducted and the follow-up 
analyses are presented in Table 2. All statistics were conducted with IBM SPSS v.25. Alpha was 
set at p < .05 for all tests (IBM, New York, NY, USA)."

Figure 1. Group centroid plot from DFA. 
 
DISCUSSION 
 
The discriminant function analysis revealed one significant function (discriminant function 
#1/DF1; Table 4) which indicated that jump height and peak power discriminate between 
female athletes at NCAA DI institutions and NAIA institutions. These two variables can be 
viewed as an athlete’s ability to propel or accelerate their body vertically off the ground and 
produce power in multiple directions (i.e. jumping, sprinting, and change of direction ability). 
The DFA follow-up ANOVA showed a significant difference between all males and females 
regardless of competition level based on the scores from the DF1. The scores of females were 
also significantly different between the two competition levels. However, male scores were not 
significantly different based on the DF1 scores. Overall DF1 had a large effect on discriminating 
between the four groups (canonical R2 = .69. This metric is used to convey the effect size). The 
results displayed in the group centroid plots (Figure 1) and the DFA follow-up ANOVA 
indicates that the significant function could be indicative of strength differences between the 
participants. The findings of this study are believed to be the first to attempt to examine 
differences in athletes from NCAA DI and NAIA institutions based on performance variables 
recorded in the CMJ. 
 
The findings of this study based on the results of the MANOVA and follow-up univariate 
ANOVAs are that females at the DI level performed significantly better in the CMJ based on 
jump height, peak power and concentric RPD-100ms compared to females at the NAIA. The 
results displayed in Table 3 show that DI females jumped roughly 5cm higher with higher power"
  },
  {
    "page": 8,
    "text": "Int J Exerc Sci 13(6): 470-479, 2020 
International Journal of Exercise Science http://www.intjexersci.com 
477 
outputs and did so faster (RPD-100ms) than their NAIA counterparts. Previous research using 
female participants at different levels of NCAA competition has shown that DI athletes across 
different sports (soccer, volleyball, softball) had greater vertical jump heights than their DII or 
DIII counterparts (3, 22). The findings in this study showed that female DI athletes differed 
significantly from their NAIA counterparts in all performance variables measured. The previous 
literature on female participants at different collegiate competition levels did not report on peak 
power or concentric RPD-100ms. However, because jump height and power are correlated 
variables it would be likely that similar results would be seen in those populations. 
 
The findings of this study showed DI male participants obtained a higher vertical jump than 
NAIA males, however the difference was roughly 1cm (Table 3). This study is believed to be the 
first study to report peak power and concentric RPD-100ms for male athletes at the NCAA DI 
and NAIA levels. Only peak power was found to be significantly different between the two 
groups of males. However, it was noted that the NCAA DI group differed significantly in body 
mass for the NAIA group (Table 1). This body mass difference is most likely the reason for the 
observed difference in peak power, and although there was a difference in body mass, both 
groups obtained nearly the same jump height. This suggests that the two groups may not be as 
different in respect to physical performance as previously thought. Previous research has shown 
that male athletes from DI have jumped higher than their counterparts at DII or DIII (9, 10). 
Brummitt & Engillis (4) found that DIII and NAIA did not differ significantly in the single leg 
hop or standing long jump. Only one study was identified which reported vertical jump 
performance comparisons between NCAA DI and NAIA male athletes (23). The DI baseball 
players obtained higher vertical jump heights than their NAIA counterparts. The results of the 
current study show that females differed from males in all variables measured regardless of 
competition level. Given that females and males differ in body mass, this variable was not 
included as a covariate. Future research comparing athletes from different competition levels 
should include body mass in the analysis. In the current study, sport was not used as a covariate 
because the group sizes (n) based on sport were small. Further research should seek to obtain a 
sufficient number of participants to include sport as a covariate. One major limitation of the 
analysis is that Box’s M was violated (p < .001) which decreases the MANOVA’s trustworthiness. 
It is important to note that Field (8) warns of the disadvantage of using Box’s M particularly that 
it is very sensitive. Furthermore, the results of the univariate and multivariate analyses, in

lines: - Design: comparison of existing archival test data collected during routine testing. The text does not say how many test sessions each athlete completed [p. 3].
- Exposure or intervention: none was applied. The grouping variables were competition level (NCAA DI vs NAIA) and sex [p. 4].
- Comparator: NAIA vs DI within each sex, and males vs females [p. 5].

-- Measurements and outcomes: CMJ on dual single-axis force plates (Pasco PS 2141, 1000 Hz, unfiltered), processed with Force-Decks software (VALD Performance) [p. 4]. Jump height was calculated from flight time as (g x t^2)/8 [p. 4]. Outcomes were jump height (cm), peak power (W) and concentric RPD-100ms (W/s). Values came from the higher of the two successful trials [p. 4]. Athlete height was recorded by staff [p. 4].

+- Measurements and outcomes: CMJ on dual single-axis force plates (Pasco PS 2141, 1000 Hz, unfiltered) [p. 3], processed with Force-Decks software (VALD Performance) [p. 4]. Jump height was calculated from flight time as (g x t^2)/8 [p. 4]. Outcomes were jump height (cm), peak power (W) and concentric RPD-100ms (W/s). Values came from the higher of the two successful trials [p. 4]. Athlete height was recorded by staff [p. 4].

- Analysis: 2 x 2 multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) for sex and competition level on the three outcomes, followed by separate ANOVAs and a discriminant function analysis (DFA). Analyses used SPSS v.25 with alpha = .05 [p. 4] [Table 2, p. 5]. A post hoc G*Power analysis reported achieved power of 0.983 and an effect size of 0.0494 [p. 3].
## Key findings

lines: - Sex and competition level together were associated with the three CMJ variables in the MANOVA: Wilks' lambda = 0.908, F(3,259) = 8.732, p < .001, partial eta-squared = .092 [p. 5] [p. 1]. This is an association across four groups, not a test of cause.

- DI females differed from NAIA females on all three variables taken together (Wilks' lambda = 0.911, F(3,259) = 8.418, p < .001, partial eta-squared = 0.089) [p. 5]. Means (SD) as printed: jump height 32.2 (4.99) cm vs 27.4 (5.17) cm; peak power 3264.3 (628.1) W vs 2835.7 (464.5) W; concentric RPD-100ms 15548.7 (702.6) W/s vs 11718.7 (4338.9) W/s [Table 3, p. 6]. The text says DI females jumped roughly 5 cm higher [p. 7].

- DI males differed from NAIA males only in peak power (Wilks' lambda = 0.955, F(3,259) = 4.096, p < .01, partial eta-squared = .045) [p. 5]. Means (SD) as printed: peak power 4888.6 (683.4) W vs 4538.6 (892.2) W; jump height 42.6 (4.75) cm vs 41.2 (6.47) cm; concentric RPD-100ms 22964.6 (7366.6) W/s vs 23160.1 (7326.7) W/s [Table 3, p. 6]. The text describes the jump height gap as roughly 1 cm [p. 8].

-- One discriminant function was significant (Wilks' lambda = .3; the test is printed as "η²(9) = 316.9", p < .001; canonical R² = .69). Its structure coefficients were jump height .861, peak power .821 and concentric RPD-100ms .479 [Table 4, p. 6]. Data check: the coefficient symbol in the text is not a standard chi-square symbol, so check the source PDF before quoting that test.

- Follow-up ANOVA on the discriminant scores: F(3,261) = 196.885, p < .001, partial eta-squared = 0.694. Both female groups differed from both male groups (p < .001). DI and NAIA females differed (p < .001). Males did not differ on these scores (p > .05) [p. 6].
- Height and weight differed by group, but age did not (height p < .001; weight p < .001; age p > .05). DI males did not differ from NAIA males in height or weight (both p > .05) [p. 6].

- Descriptive values for the pooled groups (Table 3, p. 6): DI all (n = 152) jump height 37.1 (7.51) cm, peak power 4108.5 (1045.2) W; NAIA all (n = 113) 33.6 (9.01) cm, 3604.3 (1094.2) W; females (n = 135) 29.4 (5.40) cm; males (n = 130) 42.0 (5.50) cm [Table 3, p. 6]. The authors describe the NAIA values as the first reported for that population [p. 9].

lines: ## Practitioner interpretation

-Interpretation, not a study finding. The sample is two DI universities and one NAIA university, all tested on the same force plate system and flight-time method. The values in Table 3 [p. 6] can serve as a rough reference for similar groups tested the same way, not as a standard for any individual athlete. In this sample, the DI-NAIA jump height gap was about 5 cm for females but about 1 cm for males [p. 7] [p. 8], so a single pooled reference would hide that sex difference. The data are group averages and do not show that a jump score predicts success at a level. The authors' suggestion that the discriminant function may reflect strength differences [p. 7] is speculation: no strength measure appears in the Methods [p. 3] [p. 4], so it should not be used as a practical conclusion.

Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. Volume, issue and page numbers are not finalized in the printed text ("XX(X): 000-000") [p. 1]. Year: the paper's own citation line prints 2025, while the page footers and copyright line print 2026 [p. 1] [p. 2]; the 2026 year is taken from the Zotero date. DOI from Zotero metadata.

24	## Why it was promoted
25	
26	The paper text does not state a reason for promotion. Zotero metadata places the item in the "Force Plate Practitioner" and "SecondBrain Queue" collections (metadata, not text). The paper's stated goal is to compare four common single leg countermovement jump (SLCMJ) techniques on reliability and performance, with the aim of improving test standardization for sport and rehabilitation testing [p. 2]. The concrete decision this serves is not named in the text; the likely use is choosing and fixing one SLCMJ technique for unilateral testing, which is an interpretation.
27	
28	## Research question
29	
30	The aim was to compare four SLCMJ variations (A: 90 degree hip and knee flexion, B: 90 degree knee bend, C: straight limb, D: unrestricted limb) for reliability and performance across outcome, kinetic, temporal and kinematic metrics [p. 2]. The authors hypothesised that technique D would give greater outcome values because of greater free-limb action [p. 2].
31	
32	## Population and context
33	
34	- Participants: 24 university sports science students, 19 male and 5 female, aged 18 to 35 years. Mean (SD) age 21.4 (3.7) years, height 176.0 (8.2) cm, mass 71.7 (10.8) kg [p. 1] [p. 2]. The text does not report sex-specific results.
35	- Sport and level: "diverse sports backgrounds (i.e., soccer, athletics, hockey)" with no count per sport. The authors describe the sample as amateur rather than elite [p. 2] [p. 12]. Training status was not treated as a limiting factor [p. 3].
36	- Training or return-to-play context: no injured athletes were tested. Participants were free from any injury that would prevent maximal effort trials [p. 2]. Rehabilitation use is discussed by the authors but was not tested in an injured group [p. 2] [p. 12].
37	- Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: participants completed Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaires and gave informed consent [p. 2]. Trials were excluded if the hands left the hips, the knee tucked, or the technique changed; a replacement trial was performed [p. 3]. Participants wore shorts and avoided thick-soled trainers designed for distance running [p. 2] [p. 3].
38	
39	## Study design and methods
40	
41	- Design: within-subject repeated-measures design in a single session. Each participant completed three trials of each of the four techniques, on both limbs, in randomized order [p. 2] [p. 3].
42	- Exposure or intervention: the four jump techniques. The authors say the free leg was held or swung differently across techniques; technique C held the leg straight, and technique D allowed free swing [p. 3].
43	- Comparator: the other three techniques, plus left against right limb and within-session reliability for each technique [p. 2].
44	- Measurements and outcomes: vertical ground reaction force from a single Hawkin Dynamics wireless force plate at 1000 Hz, low-pass filtered at 50 Hz [p. 3] [p. 4]. Outcomes were system weight, jump height, jump momentum, countermovement depth, time to take-off, modified reactive strength index (mRSI), braking and propulsive impulse, and peak braking and propulsive force [Table 1, p. 4]. Kinematics came from 2D video at 100 fps analysed in Quintic Biomechanics v35 [p. 3] [p. 4]. The average of three successful trials was used [p. 3] [p. 4].
45	- Analysis: SPSS v29.0. Relative reliability used a two-way mixed, absolute agreement ICC(1,3) with 95 percent CI; absolute reliability used the coefficient of variation (CV). Acceptable reliability was ICC above 0.70 and CV below 10 percent [p. 4]. Between-technique comparisons used repeated-measures ANOVA or the Friedman test, with Bonferroni post hoc tests, partial eta-squared, Cohen's d and Rosenthal's r [p. 4]. The sample size estimate used effect sizes from a prior study and required 10 to 13 participants [p. 2].
46	
47	## Key findings
48	
49	- Reliability: system weight was reliable for every technique (ICC 1.00; CV 0.09 to 0.16 percent) [Table 2, p. 6]. The Discussion says this was not influenced by technique [p. 9].
50	- Reliability of jump height was acceptable for all techniques: ICC 0.88 to 0.96 and CV 7.05 to 9.81 percent across left and right limbs [Table 2, p. 6]. The text calls absolute reliability for jump height "good" [p. 4].
51	- Technique B (90 degree knee bend) had the highest reliability across most metrics. The abstract summarises this as ICC of at least 0.80 and CV of at most 13 percent [p. 1] [p. 9]. For example, B's countermovement depth ICC was 0.96 left and 0.84 right, with CV 7.81 and 12.44 percent [Table 2, p. 6].
52	- Lowest reliability for countermovement depth was technique A, left limb: ICC 0.51 (95% CI 0.27 to 0.73), CV 24.39 percent [Table 2, p. 6] [p. 10].
53	- Time to take-off was the least reliable timing metric: technique D was rated poor [p. 4]. The Discussion says it was the lowest reliability of all variables across techniques [p. 10].
54	- Braking impulse on technique D had poor reliability: ICC 0.62 left and 0.26 right [Table 2, p. 6] [p. 10]. The authors say the other techniques had ICC of at least 0.85 [p. 10].
55	- Kinematic reliability at take-off was unacceptable for all techniques (ICC at or below 0.70). The authors attribute this to difficulty identifying the exact take-off frame on video [p. 10]. Ankle dorsiflexion at the bottom of descent was poor for techniques C and D on the right limb (ICC 0.05 and 0.00) [Table 3, p. 6].
56	- Jump height differed between techniques on the left and right limbs. Technique D was greater than A, B and C on the left (pairwise r from 0.47 to 0.79) and on the right (r from 0.70 to 0.80). Technique C was lower than A and B on the left (r = -0.60 and -0.55) [p. 5]. Per the Discussion, D was 7 percent higher than B, B was 8 percent higher than A, and A was 8 percent higher than C [p. 10]. These percentages cannot be checked from Table 4, because Table 4 reports jump height as three values per cell (described as median and interquartile range) [Table 4, p. 7].
57	- Jump momentum: technique D was higher than A and C on the left (p < .001; d = 0.93 and 1.22), and higher than A, B and C on the right [p. 5]. Left-limb descriptive values: D 124.92 (32.30), A 117.04 (30.58), B 119.77 (33.19), C 114.59 (30.34) [Table 4, p. 7].
58	- Countermovement depth differed by technique, with B deeper (about 0.17 m) than A, C and D (average about 0.14 m) [p. 11]. Time to take-off: technique C was shorter than B and D on both limbs (left: D vs C p = 0.027, d = 0.66; B vs C p = 0.022, d = 0.64; right: D vs C p = 0.023, d = 0.60; B vs C p = 0.045, d = 0.66) [p. 5] [p. 7].
59	- mRSI did not differ significantly between techniques on either limb [p. 7]. The authors note mRSI was slightly higher for technique D with small to moderate effect sizes (d between -0.23 and -0.57, sign as printed) [p. 10].
60	- Peak forces and impulses: the Discussion says technique D produced the lowest peak braking force [p. 11]. On the left limb, peak propulsive force was greater for D than B (p = 0.026, d = 0.65) and peak braking force was greater for A than D (p = 0.013, d = 0.71) [p. 8]. On the right limb, the ANOVA for peak braking force was significant but no pairwise comparison reached significance [p. 8].
61	- Kinematics at the bottom of descent: technique D had larger trunk and hip angles and larger knee flexion than the other techniques (for example, left knee flexion 123 (13) degrees for D vs 111 to 112 (9 to 10) degrees for A to C) [Table 5, p. 9] [p. 11]. The authors attribute D's higher outcome values to greater trunk and hip work from the free limb [p. 12].
62	- Descriptive system weight, mean (SD), about 713 N for all techniques and both limbs [Table 4, p. 7].
63	
64	## Limitations and applicability
65	
66	- Most participants were amateur athletes rather than elite, and the authors say their movement patterns may differ from elite athletes [p. 12].
67	- The design was within-session only. The authors say findings may not reflect consistent or long-term performance and recommend between-session testing [p. 12].
68	- The authors state that the mechanism for technique D needs confirmation with 3D motion analysis [p. 12].
69	- 79.12 percent of subjects were right-foot dominant, and the authors offer this as a possible explanation for the low countermovement depth reliability on the left limb in technique A. This is speculation [p. 10].
70	- System weight estimation: the authors note a 1 second standing period may be hard to hold still, and between-limb weight differences could affect asymmetry calculations [p. 9].
71	- Additional transfer limitations (interpretation, not author statements): the sample was 19 men and 5 women with no sex-specific results, so the female results cannot be judged. The authors' claim that technique B "maximizes single lower limb triple extension performance" [p. 12] goes beyond the metrics measured in the paper and should be read as their view.
72	- Data check: Table 4 prints a standard deviation of 0.64 for technique D left countermovement depth, which does not match the other values (about 0.05 to 0.06) [Table 4, p. 7]. This is likely a print error; check the source PDF.
73	- Data check: Table 2 prints an ICC of 0.88 with a 95 percent CI of 0.91 to 0.96 for technique A jump height, left limb. The interval does not contain the point estimate; check the source PDF [Table 2, p. 6].
74	- Data check: the printed year is 2025 in the paper's own citation line and 2026 in the footers and copyright line [p. 1] [p. 2]. Use 2026 only with that caveat.
75	
76	## Practitioner interpretation
77	
78	Interpretation, not a study finding. In this sample of 24 non-elite students tested in one session, the choice of SLCMJ technique changed jump height and some timing and force values. For jump height, the authors' reliability figures were acceptable for every technique. The technique with the most consistent results across metrics was 90 degree knee bend (B). If a practitioner tracks change or compares limbs with this test, the paper suggests fixing one technique, using clear cues, and recording which technique was used. The free-limb technique (D) gave the highest jump heights, but the paper's own text shows it works through a different movement strategy. It may suit a practitioner who wants to maximise jump height, but it is less standardised. The paper's rehabilitation recommendations come from healthy participants and should not be applied to injured athletes without further evidence. The reliability values are within-session, so they do not show how stable a technique is across weeks.

98	| Table 4 SD of 0.64 likely print error | Table 4, p. 7 | data check |
99

4	    "text": "Original Research
A Comparison of Single Leg Countermovement 
Jump Techniques on Jump Performance: 
Considerations for Test Standardization
Ava E. Staton, Jack Fahey, and Paul A. Jones
Directorate of Psychology and Sport, School of Health and Society, University of Salford, Salford, United Kingdom
Abstract
Staton, AE, Fahey, J, and Jones, PA. A comparison of single leg countermovement jump techniques on jump performance: 
considerations for test standardization. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000–000, 2025—Single leg countermovement jump (SLCMJ) 
testing is widely used in both sport performance and rehabilitation contexts. However, several inconsistent protocols and various 
jump techniques have been used across literature. Therefore, the aim of this study was to evaluate 4 variations of the SLCMJ (A: 90˚ 
hip and knee flexion, B: 90˚ knee bend, C: straight limb, D: unrestricted limb), examining the reliability and performance across 
a range of outcome, kinetic, and temporal metrics with the goal of enhancing test standardization. Twenty-four university sports 
science students (Mean 6 SD; age 5 21.4 6 3.7 years; height 5 176.0 6 8.2 cm; mass 5 71.7 6 10.8 kg) performed 3 trials of each 
technique across both limbs, while collecting vertical ground reaction forces from dual force plates and 2D video in the sagittal 
plane. Technique B demonstrated the highest reliability across most metrics when compared with other techniques (ICC $0.80, 
CV # 13%). Significant differences (p , 0.05) were observed across all techniques within certain variables. Technique D resulted in 
greater outcome measures; however, this is achieved through an entirely different strategy relying on angular momentum generated 
by the swinging free limb and greater work performed by the stance limb hip joint compared with triple lower limb flexion followed by 
extension involved in the other techniques. Consequently, technique B, limiting the contribution of the free limb, facilitates optimal 
flexion and extension of the hip, knee, and ankle, thus, is deemed more appropriate for sports performance testing and rehabilitation 
contexts.
Key Words: unilateral, vertical jump, force platform, reliability
Introduction
An increased use of objective muscle function tests is becoming 
more commonplace in sporting environments and rehabilitation 
processes, because of the advent of commercially available, por-
table, and affordable force plate systems (3,35). The counter-
movement jump (CMJ) is one of the most implemented testing 
modalities for the assessment of lower-body mechanical capaci-
ties (1). It has been commonly used for monitoring sports per-
formance (31), assessing neuromuscular fatigue and function 
(9,10), readiness to train (12), and the effectiveness of different 
training programs (5). Vertical jump actions are considered an 
essential motor skill in a range of individual and team sports 
including soccer (43), volleyball (42), basketball (50), and 
handball (24). Usually, CMJ tests are performed bilaterally; 
however, these key motor actions are typically performed uni-
laterally. Thus, unilateral vertical jump tests appear particularly 
relevant in sport-specific contexts and are notably useful during 
return-to-sport to quantify deficits or interlimb asymmetries (25) 
after a lower limb injury. Moreover, for other activities such as 
change of direction or sprinting (13,17,36), the single leg coun-
termovement jump (SLCMJ) test provides an effective indirect 
measurement of performance-based assessment (22), while eval-
uating neuromuscular capacity of the lower limbs (9).
Several studies have used the SLCMJ with different modalities 
of execution such as with or without arm swing or the free lower 
limb (40). Subsequently, the utilization and contribution of the 
free limb may modify and impact jump performance. For exam-
ple, Pamuk et al. (33) investigated the association of force-
time–related SLCMJ performance with linear sprinting and 
a T-drill, whereby subjects were required to hold the knee joint at 
90° flexion and to restrict arm swing during the jump. McElveen 
et al. (29) assessed force-time characteristics in the SLCMJ for 
several performance characteristics derived from vertical ground 
reaction forces, whereby the hip and knee of the uninvolved leg 
were held at 90° flexion to avoid ground contact, but without 
restricting arm movement. Research by Young et al. (49) dem-
onstrated greater contribution of the hip flexors when un-
restricted during the SLCMJ, and that hip flexor training may 
increase SLCMJ performance because of more powerful free leg 
actions. This may help explain the differences in average jump 
height reported between studies. For example, Pamuk et al. (33) 
reported 0.11–0.12 m among competitive elite youth male bas-
ketball players, whereas 0.15-m jump height was observed by 
McElveen et al. (29) for healthy, physically active young adults. It 
may be expected that basketball players would achieve higher 
jump heights, regardless of using arm swing.
The SLCMJ can be used to explore bilateral deficit (44) and 
between limb asymmetries (6,8), the latter of which is beneficial 
for athletes on return-to-play after injury. Van Soest et al. (44) 
examined bilateral deficit using a SLCMJ performed with the only 
instruction to keep the free leg inactive during the movement. A

Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 00(00)/1–13

5	  },
6	  {
7	    "page": 2,
8	    "text": "bilateral deficit was observed, with SLCMJ performance at 
58.5% of the (bilateral) CMJ (44). This deficit was explained by 
either greater contraction velocity of SLCMJ and/or neural 
mechanisms inhibiting the expression of maximum force during 
CMJ. Without standardization and specific control of the free 
lower limb, bilateral deficit may be amplified by the involvement 
of the free limb during the SLCMJ. In a rehabilitation context, 
Fischer et al. (16) compared isokinetic leg extension muscle 
strength and SLCMJ across anterior cruciate ligament re-
construction (ACLR) patients. However, throughout testing, 
subjects were given no clear instruction of free leg position. A lack 
of test standardization in this regard would impact between limb 
comparisons and the ability to accurately determine limb asym-
metries. This presents a problem for coaches and practitioners 
when aiming to profile injury risk, benchmark performance, and 
monitoring changes over time.
Additional literature has also acknowledged that no contri-
bution exists from the opposing limb during unilateral tests (4,8). 
However, to the best of the researchers’ knowledge, only one 
study compared different techniques of SLCMJ, specifically fo-
cusing on the contribution of the free leg (40). Schmidt et al. (40) 
investigated the effect of movement restriction of the free leg on 
SLCMJ performance and power output, comparing 2 different 
SLCMJ techniques: flexed (classic 90° knee bend technique) and 
straight (FC Luzern technique). The results of this study suggest 
that power output is higher when free leg movement is not re-
stricted (40). Greater jump height and power output in the classic 
technique were attributed to significantly greater range of motion 
of the free limb in comparison to the FC Luzern technique, with 
no difference in the range of motion of the trunk between tech-
niques (40). Despite the instruction to avoid free leg actions 
during the classic technique, this was impossible with the free leg 
flexed and performance clearly enhanced in this condition, thus, 
suggesting the FC Luzern technique may be more useful to restrict 
and standardize the position and movement of the free leg (40). 
No studies have directly compared variations of SLCMJ techni-
ques or proved the opposed free limb provides any or no contri-
bution to performance. These findings highlight the importance 
of standardizing actions of the free limb during SLCMJ to control 
compensatory movements and, thus, proper assessment of “true” 
force generated by the active lower limb. Without standardiza-
tion, reliability of SLCMJ tests could be significantly decreased 
because of such improper testing conditions and procedures, thus, 
questioning validity of SLCMJ tests when comparing with nor-
mative and benchmarking data (32).
Clearly, SLCMJ testing has numerous sports and clinical 
applications. From a practical perspective, SLCMJ tests are sim-
ple to perform, generally, nonfatiguing and time-efficient, which
are factors that should not be overlooked in sport performance 
and rehabilitation settings, especially when working with large 
squads of athletes where time constraints may preclude regular 
neuromuscular testing (7). However, numerous inconsistent 
SLCMJ protocols and techniques have been used across litera-
ture. Thus, the aim of the present study was to compare 4 com-
mon variations of SLCMJ techniques (A: 90° hip and knee, B: 90° 
knee bend, C: straight limb, D: unrestricted limb), regarding re-
liability and performance across various outcome, kinetic and 
temporal metrics, and kinematic variables. It was hypothesized 
that technique D would produce greater outcome measures be-
cause of a greater contributing free limb action.
Methods
Experimental Approach to the Problem
A within-subject repeated-measures research design was imple-
mented, whereby testing was conducted during a single session. 
Each subject performed 3 trials of 4 different SLCMJ techniques 
(Figures 2 and 3) in a randomized order to avoid order bias. Each 
subject was familiarized with the different jump techniques before 
data collection. To address the study aims and hypotheses, within 
session reliability for each dependent variable (Table 1 and 
Figure 4) within each jump technique was quantified and com-
pared between jump techniques. In addition, each dependent 
variable was compared between each jump technique. Completed 
Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaires (PARQ) and signed 
informed consent documents were obtained from all subjects 
prior to data collection. The study was preapproved by the In-
stitutional (University of Salford) Ethics Committee (application 
ID 17057) before recruitment and testing commenced.
Subjects
To determine adequate sample size for the study, G*Power soft-
ware was used (15). Using estimated effect sizes (d 5 1.01 [right 
leg] and d 5 0.87 [left leg]) from a prior study comparing jump 
height between 2 SLCMJ techniques (40), with an alpha level of 
0.05 and power of 0.80, between 10 and 13 subjects were re-
quired. Nineteen male and 5 female (age range: 18 - 35 years) 
university sports science students (Mean 6 SD; age 5 21.4 6 3.7 
years; height 5 1.76 6 0.08 m; mass 5 71.7 6 10.8 kg) with 
diverse sports backgrounds (i.e., soccer, athletics, hockey) and 
who were free from any injury that would prevent maximum 
effort trials volunteered to participate in this study. Subjects were 
instructed to wear shorts, allowing joint centers to be visible (hip, 
knee, ankle), and to refrain from wearing thick sole trainers

12	    "text": "specifically designed for distance running, during testing. Current 
training status and previous jump training experience were not 
a limiting factor in this study, because of the focus on general-
ization effects and consistent reproducibility of results.
Experimental Procedures
A single validated (3) Hawkin Dynamics wireless force plate (5th 
Generation, Westbrook, ME) collected vertical ground reaction 
forces (vGRF) at 1,000 Hz and was zeroed between each subject’s 
trial. A Panasonic Lumix FZ-200 high-speed camera (Kadoma 
City, Osaka, Japan) captured video data at 100 fps. The camera 
was set up on a tripod 4 meters from the center of the force plate, 
positioned in the sagittal plane at a height of 0.7 meters. Addi-
tional lighting from a 1500 W floodlight, positioned opposite the 
trial area, prevented darkness overcasting the subject. A 1.22 3 
1.22-m calibration frame was also recorded to scale the image 
into real life units for later use in data analysis (Figure 1).
Upon arrival, a standardized RAMP warm-up (;10 minutes), 
consisting of 3-minutes cycling and one set of 10 reps, squat jump, 
forward lunge, open/close gate, forward leg swing, lateral leg 
swing, lateral push to base, and pogo jumps, were performed by 
each subject before testing to reduce the risk of injury. A famil-
iarization of submaximal practice trials of each jump technique 
was also conducted before testing. To prevent internal threats to
validity (i.e., avoid fatigue bias and learning effects), jump order 
was randomly assigned between subjects. Each trial began with 
subjects standing centrally on the force plate with arms placed 
akimbo. A one-second quiet weighing period was held before 
executing maximum effort trials. Three maximum effort trials 
were completed, separated by a 15-second rest between each 
repetition and a 2-minute rest between each technique. This 
process was repeated on both right and left limbs across all 
techniques. Any trials that involved hands coming off the hips, 
tucking of the knee, or another jump technique were excluded 
from data analysis with a new trial performed.
Four different techniques were performed: (a) 90° hip and knee 
(Figure 2A): subjects were instructed to raise the knee and hip of 
the free leg into a 90° flexed position, ensuring the thigh was 
parallel to the floor. From this position, the subject performed 
a countermovement, followed by a maximal effort jump, with 
a verbal standardized cue: “jump as fast and as high as possible.” 
(b) 90° knee bend (Figure 2B): subjects were instructed to bend the 
knee of the free leg into a 90° flexed position. From this position, 
the subject performed a countermovement, followed by a maxi-
mal effort jump “as fast and as high as possible.” (c) Straight limb 
(Figure 2C): subjects were instructed to extend and hold the free 
leg into a straight anterior position. From this position, the subject 
performed a countermovement, followed by a maximal effort 
jump “as fast and as high as possible.” (d) Unrestricted limb 
(Figure 3): subjects were instructed to swing and drive the knee of 
the free leg upward, ensuring a smooth and controlled motion. 
Cued “jump as fast and as high as possible.”
During trials A, B, and C, subjects were instructed to avoid any 
movement or swinging of the free leg, instead maintaining the same 
position as consistently as possible throughout the task. All trials 
were monitored throughout each testing session by the lead re-
searcher (A.S.), who reviewed each trial using a video replay and 
inspected the force-time data to check for consistency between trials.
Data Analyses
A repetition performed in accordance with the specified technique 
was accepted as valid, and the average of a total of 3 successful

automatically via Hawkin Dynamics force plate software. Verti-
cal ground reaction forces were low-pass filtered at 50 Hz in 
accordance with recommendations (20). The raw data (outcome, 
kinetic, and temporal [e.g., time to take-off] metrics, Table 1) 
were exported and analyzed via an Excel spreadsheet (Microsoft 
Corp., Redmond, WA), whereby descriptive measures were cal-
culated (mean 6 standard deviation (SD)). Kinematic parameters 
were calculated via video analyses through Quintic Biomechanics 
v35 (Solihull, United Kingdom). All trials were analyzed for 
subsequent statistical analyses. Digitization of the calibration 
frame scaled the image into real life units. Four angles were de-
termined at the bottom of descent (Figure 4A) including trunk 
flexion and hip flexion relative to the vertical, ankle dorsiflexion 
relative to the horizontal and knee flexion. Two angles were de-
termined at take-off (Figure 4B) including trunk flexion and hip 
flexion relative to the vertical. All angles generated were directly 
inputted and organized into a custom Excel spreadsheet (Micro-
soft Corp., Redmond, WA), whereby descriptive measures were 
calculated (mean 6 SD).
Statistical Analyses
Statistical analyses were conducted via SPSS Statistics v29.0 (IBM 
Corp., Chicago, IL). A 2-way mixed effect, absolute agreement 
(1,3) intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) with 95% confidence 
intervals (95% CI) was used to assess relative reliability. Absolute 
reliability was assessed by coefficient of variation (CV). Re-
liability was considered acceptable with ICC values greater than 
0.70 (23) and CV values less than 10% (12). Intraclass correlation 
coefficient values were interpreted based on the lower bound CI 
(ICC; poor ,0.49, moderate 0.50–0.74, good 0.75–0.89, and 
excellent .0.90) as suggested by Koo and Li (23). Coefficient of 
variation values were interpreted as poor $15%, moderate 
10–15%, good 5–10%, and excellent #5% (34). Normality for 
each variable was inspected using a Shapiro-Wilk test, with sig-
nificance level at p . 0.05. If parametric, a one-way repeated 
measures ANOVA was conducted to compare each variable be-
tween each technique. Partial eta squared (h 2 ) effect sizes were 
reported when significant differences occurred, interpreted as 
small 5 0.01, moderate 5 0.06, and large 5 0.14 (11). A Bon-
ferroni Post Hoc Test was used to locate significant differences, 
and Cohen’s d effect size was determined (11). If nonparametric, 
a Friedman test was conducted to analyze whether there were 
significant differences between techniques. A Wilcoxon Signed 
Ranks Test with p values Bonferroni corrected was then con-
ducted to locate any significant differences, and Rosenthal’s r 
effect sizes (r 5 Z/√N) were determined (37). Effect sizes for 
pairwise comparisons were interpreted as small (0.2), moderate 
(0.5), and large (0.8) (11).

angle at bottom of descent showed moderate relative and excel-
lent absolute reliability, with poor relative reliability observed for

42	    "text": "and performance across a range of outcome, kinetic and temporal 
metrics, and kinematic variables, with the goal of enhancing test 
standardization for consistent application in various sports per-
formance and clinical rehabilitation contexts. The main findings 
from this study revealed excellent-to-good relative and absolute 
reliability within kinetic and outcome metrics, and good-to-
moderate relative and absolute reliability within temporal metrics 
across all techniques, with only a few exceptions. Technique B: 
90° knee bend, demonstrated the highest reliability across most 
metrics when compared with other techniques. Consistent with 
the study hypothesis, the results demonstrated that outcome 
values (jump height and jump momentum) were highest when free 
limb actions were not restricted (technique D). The higher values 
observed for technique D coincide with greater angular range of 
motion in the trunk and hip, facilitated by the motion of the free 
limb. These results suggest that the choice of technique does in-
fluence performance outcomes.
One consideration of using SLCMJ tests is whether subjects 
can obtain an accurate and consistent system weight estimate 
before the jump. Using the Hawkin dynamics system enables 
system weight to be estimated from 1 second of standing before 
executing the jump, which allows the variety of variables to be 
determined. This avoids the need for extra data collection of 
system weight from a bipedal stance, saving time during athlete 
performance testing sessions. Many subjects may struggle to 
maintain balance and essentially remain still during this weighing
period before commencing the jump. A lack of stability during 
this period may lead to errors in determining subjects’ weight, 
which will subsequently impact outcome measurements when 
using the impulse-momentum method. Furthermore, between 
limb differences in system weight estimate may further impact 
between limb comparisons and calculation of asymmetry (e.g., 
using jump height), which is important when profiling injury risk 
for athletes including return to play scenarios. The results from 
the study demonstrated perfect ICCs (ICC 5 1) and low CV 
(CV , 1%) regardless of technique used. These findings are 
consistent with previous literature, as Fahey et al. (14) found 
SLCMJ system weight demonstrated excellent relative and ab-
solute reliability (lower (95% confidence interval) bound 
ICC 5 $0.90, upper (95% confidence interval) bound 
CV ,1%). However, it is important to note that subjects were 
only instructed to “jump as high and as fast as possible” and no 
specific technique was stated and used within the study. No sig-
nificant differences were reported between techniques within the 
present study, and thus, system weight estimates were reliable and 
not influenced by jump technique used, suggesting using the 
impulse-momentum method to determine SLCMJ variables can 
be effectively applied to evaluate single limb performance and 
between limb asymmetries. However, future research should 
combine bilateral and single limb jump tests to see if system 
weight measures from single leg balancing are different to bi-
lateral stance to fully eradicate this concern with SLCMJ testing.

    "text": "Original Research
A Comparison of Single Leg Countermovement 
Jump Techniques on Jump Performance: 
Considerations for Test Standardization
Ava E. Staton, Jack Fahey, and Paul A. Jones
Directorate of Psychology and Sport, School of Health and Society, University of Salford, Salford, United Kingdom
Abstract
Staton, AE, Fahey, J, and Jones, PA. A comparison of single leg countermovement jump techniques on jump performance: 
considerations for test standardization. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000–000, 2025—Single leg countermovement jump (SLCMJ) 
testing is widely used in both sport performance and rehabilitation contexts. However, several inconsistent protocols and various 
jump techniques have been used across literature. Therefore, the aim of this study was to evaluate 4 variations of the SLCMJ (A: 90˚ 
hip and knee flexion, B: 90˚ knee bend, C: straight limb, D: unrestricted limb), examining the reliability and performance across 
a range of outcome, kinetic, and temporal metrics with the goal of enhancing test standardization. Twenty-four university sports 
science students (Mean 6 SD; age 5 21.4 6 3.7 years; height 5 176.0 6 8.2 cm; mass 5 71.7 6 10.8 kg) performed 3 trials of each 
technique across both limbs, while collecting vertical ground reaction forces from dual force plates and 2D video in the sagittal 
plane. Technique B demonstrated the highest reliability across most metrics when compared with other techniques (ICC $0.80, 
CV # 13%). Significant differences (p , 0.05) were observed across all techniques within certain variables. Technique D resulted in 
greater outcome measures; however, this is achieved through an entirely different strategy relying on angular momentum generated 
by the swinging free limb and greater work performed by the stance limb hip joint compared with triple lower limb flexion followed by 
extension involved in the other techniques. Consequently, technique B, limiting the contribution of the free limb, facilitates optimal 
flexion and extension of the hip, knee, and ankle, thus, is deemed more appropriate for sports performance testing and rehabilitation 
contexts.
Key Words: unilateral, vertical jump, force platform, reliability
Introduction
An increased use of objective muscle function tests is becoming 
more commonplace in sporting environments and rehabilitation 
processes, because of the advent of commercially available, por-
table, and affordable force plate systems (3,35). The counter-
movement jump (CMJ) is one of the most implemented testing 
modalities for the assessment of lower-body mechanical capaci-
ties (1). It has been commonly used for monitoring sports per-
formance (31), assessing neuromuscular fatigue and function 
(9,10), readiness to train (12), and the effectiveness of different 
training programs (5). Vertical jump actions are considered an 
essential motor skill in a range of individual and team sports 
including soccer (43), volleyball (42), basketball (50), and 
handball (24). Usually, CMJ tests are performed bilaterally; 
however, these key motor actions are typically performed uni-
laterally. Thus, unilateral vertical jump tests appear particularly 
relevant in sport-specific contexts and are notably useful during 
return-to-sport to quantify deficits or interlimb asymmetries (25) 
after a lower limb injury. Moreover, for other activities such as 
change of direction or sprinting (13,17,36), the single leg coun-
termovement jump (SLCMJ) test provides an effective indirect 
measurement of performance-based assessment (22), while eval-
uating neuromuscular capacity of the lower limbs (9).
Several studies have used the SLCMJ with different modalities 
of execution such as with or without arm swing or the free lower 
limb (40). Subsequently, the utilization and contribution of the 
free limb may modify and impact jump performance. For exam-
ple, Pamuk et al. (33) investigated the association of force-
time–related SLCMJ performance with linear sprinting and 
a T-drill, whereby subjects were required to hold the knee joint at 
90° flexion and to restrict arm swing during the jump. McElveen 
et al. (29) assessed force-time characteristics in the SLCMJ for 
several performance characteristics derived from vertical ground 
reaction forces, whereby the hip and knee of the uninvolved leg 
were held at 90° flexion to avoid ground contact, but without 
restricting arm movement. Research by Young et al. (49) dem-
onstrated greater contribution of the hip flexors when un-
restricted during the SLCMJ, and that hip flexor training may 
increase SLCMJ performance because of more powerful free leg 
actions. This may help explain the differences in average jump 
height reported between studies. For example, Pamuk et al. (33) 
reported 0.11–0.12 m among competitive elite youth male bas-
ketball players, whereas 0.15-m jump height was observed by 
McElveen et al. (29) for healthy, physically active young adults. It 
may be expected that basketball players would achieve higher 
jump heights, regardless of using arm swing.
The SLCMJ can be used to explore bilateral deficit (44) and 
between limb asymmetries (6,8), the latter of which is beneficial 
for athletes on return-to-play after injury. Van Soest et al. (44) 
examined bilateral deficit using a SLCMJ performed with the only 
instruction to keep the free leg inactive during the movement. A

  {
    "page": 2,
    "text": "bilateral deficit was observed, with SLCMJ performance at 
58.5% of the (bilateral) CMJ (44). This deficit was explained by 
either greater contraction velocity of SLCMJ and/or neural 
mechanisms inhibiting the expression of maximum force during 
CMJ. Without standardization and specific control of the free 
lower limb, bilateral deficit may be amplified by the involvement 
of the free limb during the SLCMJ. In a rehabilitation context, 
Fischer et al. (16) compared isokinetic leg extension muscle 
strength and SLCMJ across anterior cruciate ligament re-
construction (ACLR) patients. However, throughout testing, 
subjects were given no clear instruction of free leg position. A lack 
of test standardization in this regard would impact between limb 
comparisons and the ability to accurately determine limb asym-
metries. This presents a problem for coaches and practitioners 
when aiming to profile injury risk, benchmark performance, and 
monitoring changes over time.
Additional literature has also acknowledged that no contri-
bution exists from the opposing limb during unilateral tests (4,8). 
However, to the best of the researchers’ knowledge, only one 
study compared different techniques of SLCMJ, specifically fo-
cusing on the contribution of the free leg (40). Schmidt et al. (40) 
investigated the effect of movement restriction of the free leg on 
SLCMJ performance and power output, comparing 2 different 
SLCMJ techniques: flexed (classic 90° knee bend technique) and 
straight (FC Luzern technique). The results of this study suggest 
that power output is higher when free leg movement is not re-
stricted (40). Greater jump height and power output in the classic 
technique were attributed to significantly greater range of motion 
of the free limb in comparison to the FC Luzern technique, with 
no difference in the range of motion of the trunk between tech-
niques (40). Despite the instruction to avoid free leg actions 
during the classic technique, this was impossible with the free leg 
flexed and performance clearly enhanced in this condition, thus, 
suggesting the FC Luzern technique may be more useful to restrict 
and standardize the position and movement of the free leg (40). 
No studies have directly compared variations of SLCMJ techni-
ques or proved the opposed free limb provides any or no contri-
bution to performance. These findings highlight the importance 
of standardizing actions of the free limb during SLCMJ to control 
compensatory movements and, thus, proper assessment of “true” 
force generated by the active lower limb. Without standardiza-
tion, reliability of SLCMJ tests could be significantly decreased 
because of such improper testing conditions and procedures, thus, 
questioning validity of SLCMJ tests when comparing with nor-
mative and benchmarking data (32).
Clearly, SLCMJ testing has numerous sports and clinical 
applications. From a practical perspective, SLCMJ tests are sim-
ple to perform, generally, nonfatiguing and time-efficient, which
are factors that should not be overlooked in sport performance 
and rehabilitation settings, especially when working with large 
squads of athletes where time constraints may preclude regular 
neuromuscular testing (7). However, numerous inconsistent 
SLCMJ protocols and techniques have been used across litera-
ture. Thus, the aim of the present study was to compare 4 com-
mon variations of SLCMJ techniques (A: 90° hip and knee, B: 90° 
knee bend, C: straight limb, D: unrestricted limb), regarding re-
liability and performance across various outcome, kinetic and 
temporal metrics, and kinematic variables. It was hypothesized 
that technique D would produce greater outcome measures be-
cause of a greater contributing free limb action.
Methods
Experimental Approach to the Problem
A within-subject repeated-measures research design was imple-
mented, whereby testing was conducted during a single session. 
Each subject performed 3 trials of 4 different SLCMJ techniques 
(Figures 2 and 3) in a randomized order to avoid order bias. Each 
subject was familiarized with the different jump techniques before 
data collection. To address the study aims and hypotheses, within 
session reliability for each dependent variable (Table 1 and 
Figure 4) within each jump technique was quantified and com-
pared between jump techniques. In addition, each dependent 
variable was compared between each jump technique. Completed 
Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaires (PARQ) and signed 
informed consent documents were obtained from all subjects 
prior to data collection. The study was preapproved by the In-
stitutional (University of Salford) Ethics Committee (application 
ID 17057) before recruitment and testing commenced.
Subjects
To determine adequate sample size for the study, G*Power soft-
ware was used (15). Using estimated effect sizes (d 5 1.01 [right 
leg] and d 5 0.87 [left leg]) from a prior study comparing jump 
height between 2 SLCMJ techniques (40), with an alpha level of 
0.05 and power of 0.80, between 10 and 13 subjects were re-
quired. Nineteen male and 5 female (age range: 18 - 35 years) 
university sports science students (Mean 6 SD; age 5 21.4 6 3.7 
years; height 5 1.76 6 0.08 m; mass 5 71.7 6 10.8 kg) with 
diverse sports backgrounds (i.e., soccer, athletics, hockey) and 
who were free from any injury that would prevent maximum 
effort trials volunteered to participate in this study. Subjects were 
instructed to wear shorts, allowing joint centers to be visible (hip, 
knee, ankle), and to refrain from wearing thick sole trainers

    "text": "specifically designed for distance running, during testing. Current 
training status and previous jump training experience were not 
a limiting factor in this study, because of the focus on general-
ization effects and consistent reproducibility of results.
Experimental Procedures
A single validated (3) Hawkin Dynamics wireless force plate (5th 
Generation, Westbrook, ME) collected vertical ground reaction 
forces (vGRF) at 1,000 Hz and was zeroed between each subject’s 
trial. A Panasonic Lumix FZ-200 high-speed camera (Kadoma 
City, Osaka, Japan) captured video data at 100 fps. The camera 
was set up on a tripod 4 meters from the center of the force plate, 
positioned in the sagittal plane at a height of 0.7 meters. Addi-
tional lighting from a 1500 W floodlight, positioned opposite the 
trial area, prevented darkness overcasting the subject. A 1.22 3 
1.22-m calibration frame was also recorded to scale the image 
into real life units for later use in data analysis (Figure 1).
Upon arrival, a standardized RAMP warm-up (;10 minutes), 
consisting of 3-minutes cycling and one set of 10 reps, squat jump, 
forward lunge, open/close gate, forward leg swing, lateral leg 
swing, lateral push to base, and pogo jumps, were performed by 
each subject before testing to reduce the risk of injury. A famil-
iarization of submaximal practice trials of each jump technique 
was also conducted before testing. To prevent internal threats to
validity (i.e., avoid fatigue bias and learning effects), jump order 
was randomly assigned between subjects. Each trial began with 
subjects standing centrally on the force plate with arms placed 
akimbo. A one-second quiet weighing period was held before 
executing maximum effort trials. Three maximum effort trials 
were completed, separated by a 15-second rest between each 
repetition and a 2-minute rest between each technique. This 
process was repeated on both right and left limbs across all 
techniques. Any trials that involved hands coming off the hips, 
tucking of the knee, or another jump technique were excluded 
from data analysis with a new trial performed.
Four different techniques were performed: (a) 90° hip and knee 
(Figure 2A): subjects were instructed to raise the knee and hip of 
the free leg into a 90° flexed position, ensuring the thigh was 
parallel to the floor. From this position, the subject performed 
a countermovement, followed by a maximal effort jump, with 
a verbal standardized cue: “jump as fast and as high as possible.” 
(b) 90° knee bend (Figure 2B): subjects were instructed to bend the 
knee of the free leg into a 90° flexed position. From this position, 
the subject performed a countermovement, followed by a maxi-
mal effort jump “as fast and as high as possible.” (c) Straight limb 
(Figure 2C): subjects were instructed to extend and hold the free 
leg into a straight anterior position. From this position, the subject 
performed a countermovement, followed by a maximal effort 
jump “as fast and as high as possible.” (d) Unrestricted limb 
(Figure 3): subjects were instructed to swing and drive the knee of 
the free leg upward, ensuring a smooth and controlled motion. 
Cued “jump as fast and as high as possible.”
During trials A, B, and C, subjects were instructed to avoid any 
movement or swinging of the free leg, instead maintaining the same 
position as consistently as possible throughout the task. All trials 
were monitored throughout each testing session by the lead re-
searcher (A.S.), who reviewed each trial using a video replay and 
inspected the force-time data to check for consistency between trials.
Data Analyses
A repetition performed in accordance with the specified technique 
was accepted as valid, and the average of a total of 3 successful
